Name: cultural_default_switch
Title: The Cultural Default Switch: How Multilingual LLMs Silently Change Their Answers to Underspecified Questions Based on Query Language
Short Hypothesis: When multilingual LLMs answer culturally/contextually underspecified questions (e.g., 'What is a typical breakfast?', 'What color is a wedding dress?', 'What is the legal drinking age?'), they resolve the ambiguity using priors tied to the query language rather than a fixed universal default. We hypothesize that (1) this language-conditioned default resolution is systematic and predictable from the cultural region associated with each language, (2) it is controlled by a compact, causally identifiable 'cultural context' direction in the residual stream that is largely separate from factual-knowledge subspaces, and (3) this direction can be causally steered to decouple the model's cultural default from its query language, enabling a query in one language to produce answers grounded in a different cultural context on demand.
Related Work: Prior work studies cross-lingual factual consistency (Qi et al. 2023 RankC), cross-lingual knowledge editing/propagation (X-KDE, MPN, XME, CLM-Bench), and language-specific vs shared neurons (Riemenschneider & Frank 2025; Mondal et al. 2025). CLM-Bench shows factual edit vectors are near-orthogonal across languages. All of these treat knowledge as having a single correct answer and measure whether it propagates or stays consistent. Our work targets a fundamentally different phenomenon: underspecified questions that have NO single correct answer, where the model must supply an implicit cultural/contextual default. We ask whether the query language acts as a hidden 'context switch' selecting culturally appropriate priors, whether this is a separable causal direction (distinct from factual subspaces), and whether it can be independently steered. This reframes multilingual variation as legitimate context-conditioning rather than inconsistency-to-be-fixed, and provides a controllability handle absent in editing/consistency literature.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs are usually evaluated on questions with unique correct answers, where cross-lingual variation is treated as inconsistency to be minimized. But many everyday questions are underspecified and have no single right answer: a typical breakfast, an appropriate gift, the legal drinking age, or the color of a wedding dress all depend on unstated cultural context. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs treat the query language as a hidden 'cultural default switch', silently resolving such underspecification using priors associated with the language's dominant cultural region. We construct a benchmark of culturally-underspecified questions with region-grounded reference distributions, and measure how a model's answers shift across ten languages spanning diverse cultural regions and scripts. We then test whether this behavior is mediated by a compact, causally identifiable 'cultural context' direction in the residual stream, extracted via difference-of-means over parallel same-content prompts, and whether it is separable from factual-knowledge subspaces (comparing to edit-vector geometry). Finally, we show that steering this direction lets a query in one language yield answers grounded in a chosen alternative cultural context, decoupling default resolution from surface language. Across four open models we quantify how strongly language conditions defaults, how this scales with cultural distance, and how faithfully the effect can be causally controlled. This reframes multilingual variation on ambiguous inputs as controllable context-conditioning rather than error, with implications for cultural fairness, localization, and interpretability.
Experiments: 1) Benchmark construction: Curate ~300 culturally-underspecified questions across domains (food, dress/color conventions, etiquette/gift-giving, legal/regulatory defaults like drinking/voting age, holidays, units/currency defaults, name conventions). For each, define region-conditioned reference answer distributions from World Values Survey / Wikipedia / country-fact sources (e.g., expected drinking age per region). Translate to 10 languages spanning distinct cultural regions and scripts (English, Spanish, French, German, Russian, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili), with native/MT verification. 2) Behavioral measurement: On open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B), sample K answers per (question, language); classify each answer to a cultural-region label (via a classifier / rule matching against region references). Compute per-language default distribution and a Cultural-Default-Alignment score = agreement between the model's modal default and the language's dominant-region reference. 3) Distance modeling: Regress cross-language default divergence (JS divergence between per-language answer distributions) on cultural distance (e.g., WVS cultural-map coordinates, geographic/religious features) and script overlap; report Spearman correlations. 4) Causal direction extraction: For each ordered language pair (L_a, L_b), compute a 'cultural context' direction as difference-of-means of mid-layer residual-stream activations over parallel same-content underspecified prompts. Test whether a single low-rank subspace captures cultural switching across many pairs (PCA on pairwise directions). 5) Separability from facts: Extract factual edit/language vectors on the same models (using CounterFact-style unique-answer items) and measure cosine/subspace overlap between the 'cultural default' subspace and factual-language subspaces; hypothesis is low overlap. 6) Causal steering: Add the L_a->L_b cultural direction at mid layers when querying in L_a; measure the fraction of answers whose cultural-region label shifts toward L_b's default (steering success), while a control set of unique-answer factual questions should remain unchanged (specificity). 7) Ablations: layer selection, steering strength, low-rank vs full direction; manipulation checks that steering does not just switch the surface output language. Metrics: Cultural-Default-Alignment, cross-language JS divergence, cultural-distance correlation, subspace overlap with factual directions, steering success rate, factual-specificity retention, fluency filter pass rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Region-conditioned reference distributions are approximations and may embed their own biases; we source from multiple datasets and report sensitivity. 2) Answer-to-region classification can be noisy for open-ended text; mitigate with structured/short-answer prompting and manual validation on a subset. 3) Models may default to a single dominant (often US/English) culture regardless of query language, weakening the 'switch' claim; this null result is itself informative (evidence of monocultural default) and detectable by our design. 4) Difference-of-means directions may entangle language identity with cultural context; we control content via parallel translations and include a language-only steering baseline to disentangle. 5) Cultural distance metrics (WVS coordinates) are imperfect proxies; we triangulate with geographic and religious feature distances. 6) Effects may be model-specific; we report across four models to assess generality.
